questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/0abae6be42361d157d7cbd46f602d3a0d2044cfec551c61a2739ff9b56798cc3.png)

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Which of the following gives an expression for the lower Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: ${m}_{ij}$ denotes the minimum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}$*
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the lower Riemann sum $L$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $3$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{m}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ denotes the minimum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
L={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{m}_{13}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{13}).
$$

Notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{12})=\text{Area}({R}_{13})=3.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =3\cdot {m}_{11}+3\cdot {m}_{12}+3\cdot {m}_{13} \\  & =3({m}_{11}+{m}_{12}+{m}_{13}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the lower Riemann sum $L$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $4$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{m}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ denotes the minimum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
L={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{m}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{m}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22}).
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{12})=1,
$$

and

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{21})=\text{Area}({R}_{22})=2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =1\cdot {m}_{11}+2\cdot {m}_{21}+1\cdot {m}_{12}+2\cdot {m}_{22} \\  & ={m}_{11}+2{m}_{21}+{m}_{12}+2{m}_{22}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Lower Riemann Sum for a Strictly Decreasing Function
questions.problem:
Let $R=[0,2]\times [0,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=5-x-y.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={0,1,2},\,{P}_{2}={0,1,2},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the lower Riemann sum $L(f,P).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/3cac974f7352243bfbe008ad8af58ae8222709f81f434070383cc759a46747c7.png)

The lower Riemann sum $L(f,P)$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{m}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{m}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22})
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the minimum value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=1$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $L(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
L(f,P)={m}_{11}+{m}_{21}+{m}_{12}+{m}_{22}.
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=5-x-y$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=5-x-y$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/0fefe892c74e8d391e56ee822f83e7e0fe0110593c9d6a4b93b8cfe1e558ab16.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/fe872f1f1b0307760dcdba6ac6f6be20f197662ac250ab46dc77fa472295906f.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{11} & =f(1,1)=3 \\ {m}_{21} & =f(2,1)=2 \\ {m}_{12} & =f(1,2)=2 \\ {m}_{22} & =f(2,2)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
L(f,P)=3+2+2+1=8.
$$

questions.problem:
Let $R=[0,4]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=13-x-{y}^{2}.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={0,1,2,3,4},\,{P}_{2}={1,3},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the lower Riemann sum $L(f,P).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/48356d566752c064e9381c2f9ce27ef12bbdd86a29a2dab0d3dda05088630006.png)

The lower Riemann sum $L(f,P)$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{m}_{31}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{31})+{m}_{41}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{41})
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the minimum value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=2$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $L(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
L(f,P)=2{m}_{11}+2{m}_{21}+2{m}_{31}+2{m}_{41}.
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=13-x-{y}^{2}$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=13-x-{y}^{2}$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/90ed44b97d085413780f2dce297dd78ffa4c968a244e73c431d2e9aa30e14d22.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/860ba8cf7e5135f7e2eedcde7534fe9880feb38c29163625e32b79f18fce2f2f.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{11} & =f(1,3)=3 \\ {m}_{21} & =f(2,3)=2 \\ {m}_{31} & =f(3,3)=1 \\ {m}_{41} & =f(4,3)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
L(f,P)=2\cdot 3+2\cdot 2+2\cdot 1+2\cdot 0=12.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Expression for the Lower Bounds
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072149/assets/8de3a1512666201ab8d9ab7c06385dac08acb67345273a2e07252616f666cf27.png)

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Express the lower Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the lower Riemann sum $L$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $4$ rectangular solids, one for each $R_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion $R_{ij}$ is given by

$$
m_{ij}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{ij})
$$

where $m_{ij}$ denotes the minimum value of $f$ on the subregion $R_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
L = m_{11}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{11}) + m_{21}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{21}) + m_{12}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{12}) + m_{22}\cdot \textrm{Area}(R_{22}).
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\textrm{Area}(R_{11}) = \textrm{Area}(R_{21}) = 3
$$

and

$$
\textrm{Area}(R_{12}) = \textrm{Area}(R_{22}) = 1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =3\cdot {m}_{11}+3\cdot {m}_{21}+{m}_{12}+{m}_{22} \\  & =3{m}_{11}+3{m}_{21}+{m}_{12}+{m}_{22}.\end{aligned}
$$
